claude_result.result: {"answers":{"q1":"Under the current design the steward chooses the subsequent work, not the orchestrator, even when the operator instructs the orchestrator to create replacement work (steward-next-work, status accepted/current, sourced from source-2; link steward-next-work governs choose-next-work; steward-role). The needed distinction is between deciding which work pursues the intention (the 'choose-next-work' operation, owned by steward) and mechanically inserting a record (choose-next-work text). The orchestrator may end the failed attempt as a 'failed' terminal result and return it to steward, or ask 'keep trying versus mark failed', but the choice of next work stays with steward (source-2; steward-next-work rationale). The operator-approved path that would let the orchestrator bypass steward is withdrawn (replacement-exception, status withdrawn/historical). Also, ending the failed attempt does not satisfy or withdraw the underlying intention, so the performance concern remains for steward to address (concern-persists, accepted/current).","q2":"Yes. Two related historical positions were considered: (a) operator-approved orchestrator replacement could bypass steward (replacement-exception, withdrawn), with the rationale of avoiding a relay when the orchestrator already had the context (source-1; replacement-exception rationale); and (b) replacement as an atomic archive/add that would not wake steward until the new work completed (atomic-replacement, withdrawn; source-1, source-2). Both were revised by steward-next-work (links 'revises'). They changed because Blake later chose the simpler rule that the steward always chooses the work, keeping one owner of the next-work choice and a clean responsibility boundary, with the orchestrator limited to asking keep-trying-versus-mark-failed (source-2; steward-next-work rationale; atomic-replacement rationale). Evidence is session paraphrase only (limitation).","q3":"No, the current theory does not establish a requirement for operator permission each time.
